897.title: Herod's Temple
897.hook: a hard king rebuilds the Temple, and one of its great outer walls still stands
897.howItsDone: Jews pray at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, and visitors leave folded written prayers in the cracks between its stones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dead Sea Scrolls: old words kept in the dark near the Dead Sea until they were found again. Your line was hidden in caves. Did something tucked away turn up for you? Today a new part of the story opens: Rome, destruction, and the rabbis. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

Folded slips of paper, pushed into the cracks between huge pale stones. Small green plants growing out of the joints. Some people press their foreheads to the stone. Some stand back and read psalms from a small book. Some just lay a hand flat on the wall and stay a while. This is the Western Wall in Jerusalem, in Hebrew the Kotel. It isn't the Temple itself. It's part of the great outer wall that held up the platform the Temple once stood on. To understand why people come to a retaining wall to pray, go back to the man who had it built. His name was Herod.
screen: `PAPERS IN THE CRACKS.` → `NOT THE TEMPLE, BUT ITS WALL.` → `GO BACK TO HEROD.`

segments.voice: Herod was a king of Judea who ruled with Rome's backing. The Jewish historian Josephus tells his story in detail, and it isn't gentle. Herod was suspicious and violent; Josephus records that he had members of his own family put to death. And this same king set out to rebuild the Second Temple, the house that had stood since the return from Babylon. Josephus describes the hill being enlarged, enormous walls raised around it to hold up a wide, level court, and a sanctuary so covered in gold and white stone that from far off it looked like a snowy mountain. The rabbis of the Talmud tell a harder story about how it began. In the tractate Bava Batra, Herod has killed the sages. One survives, Bava ben Buta, whom Herod has blinded. Herod, in disguise, tries to trick him into cursing the king. He won't. Herod then asks him what a man like himself could do to make amends, and the old sage answers, in paraphrase: you darkened the light of the world, so go and tend the light of the world. Rebuild the Temple. And the same page keeps a saying, in paraphrase: whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building. A cruel king. A beautiful house. The rabbis keep both facts and smooth over neither. The sanctuary itself would not last. But part of the western retaining wall did. One midrash reads a line from the Song of Songs, "behold, he standeth behind our wall", and says God's presence never leaves the Western Wall. The Hebrew word for wall in that verse is the same word people use for the Kotel.
screen: `A HARD KING REBUILDS THE TEMPLE.` · `A BLINDED SAGE SAYS: TEND THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `NEVER SEEN A BEAUTIFUL BUILDING.` · then: `"BEHIND OUR WALL."`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look at the wall. Close your eyes and hold the scene, or, if a screen is nearby, find a picture of the Western Wall: big pale stones, a few plants in the joints, folded papers tucked between. Pick one stone and stay with it. Someone cut it for Herod. Many hands have touched it since. Let your breath slow while you look. Then think of one thing in your own life that remained after something larger was gone: a recipe that outlived a kitchen, a habit someone taught you, a photograph. If you pray, you can say a psalm you know, the way people do at the wall. The bell holds the time.
Herod's Temple. Rebuilt by a hard king, praised even by the rabbis who remembered his cruelty, and part of its western wall still stands. Today's word.
Your line: the wall remains. Today, notice one thing that outlasted something bigger, and give it a moment of your attention. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

898.title: Two schools
898.hook: the houses of Hillel and Shammai argue, and the Talmud keeps both sides
898.howItsDone: Jewish study often happens in pairs, and the Talmud records minority opinions, including those of the house of Shammai, alongside the law that was followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's Temple: a hard king, a beautiful house, and a western wall that still stands. Your line was the wall remains. What did you notice that outlasted something bigger? Today, two teachers and the schools that grew around them. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Who gets to be right when two serious people disagree? A man comes to a teacher named Shammai with a challenge: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai, the Talmud says, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick in his hand. The man goes to another teacher, Hillel, and asks the same thing. Hillel answers, in paraphrase: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn it. Two teachers, two temperaments. Around them grew two schools, and their arguments fill page after page of the rabbis' writings.
screen: `THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT?` → `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.` → `HILLEL: GO AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're called Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai. A house here means a school: the students and their students after them. They disagreed about real things. What blessing comes first on a Friday night. How to light the Hanukkah lamps. Whether you must lie down to say the evening Shema. The house of Shammai often takes the stricter side, but the Mishnah keeps a list of cases where it's the other way. Then comes the famous passage in the tractate Eruvin. The Talmud says the two houses argued for three years, each saying the law follows us. Finally a voice from heaven spoke, in paraphrase: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the house of Hillel. Both are the words of the living God. So why Hillel? The Talmud's answer isn't that they were smarter. It's that they were gentle and patient. They taught their own view and the view of the house of Shammai, and they even mentioned Shammai's view before their own. The law went to the people who listened best. And there's a postscript. A teaching in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, says an argument for the sake of heaven will last, and its example is Hillel and Shammai. The argument itself is kept, honored, studied. The losing side isn't erased. Its words are still printed, still read, and some readers say that keeping them is a kind of respect: the minority view sits on the page right beside the majority, for anyone who comes later.
screen: `BEIT HILLEL AND BEIT SHAMMAI.` · then, large: `THESE AND THESE ARE THE WORDS OF GOD.` · `THE LAW FOLLOWS THE GENTLER HOUSE.` · then: `AN ARGUMENT FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to honor someone who thinks the opposite. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Choose one person who sees something very differently than you do: politics, faith, how to raise kids, how to load a dishwasher. Try the house of Hillel's habit. Say their view to yourself first, as fairly as you can, in words they would recognize. Then say your own. Notice what changes when their side gets spoken first. You don't have to agree. If you pray, you can hold them in that prayer by name. The bell holds the time.
Two schools. The house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, whose arguments the Talmud keeps side by side, and whose law goes to the house that listened. Today's word.
Your line: the house of hillel. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's view back to them before you give your own. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

899.title: The Great Revolt (66–70 CE)
899.hook: a revolt against Rome ends with Jerusalem and the Temple burned
899.howItsDone: Jews mark the fall of both Temples on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, with a fast, by sitting low like mourners, and by reading the book of Lamentations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two schools, and a heavenly voice that called both sides the words of the living God. Your line was the house of hillel. Did you say someone's view back to them first? Today, the city those teachers lived in goes up in flames. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

A man in Jerusalem throws a party. He tells his servant to invite his friend Kamtza. The servant brings Bar Kamtza instead, a man the host can't stand. The host orders him out. Bar Kamtza begs: let me stay, I'll pay for what I eat. Half the feast. The whole feast. No. He is thrown out in front of everyone, and the rabbis at the table say nothing. That's how the Talmud begins its story of the fall of Jerusalem. Not with armies. With a guest list.
screen: `THE WRONG GUEST.` → `THROWN OUT IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` → `THE RABBIS SAY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The history comes to us mainly through Josephus, a Jewish commander in the war who later wrote its story under Roman patronage. Judea was ruled by Rome, the governors were harsh, and the people were split among themselves. Revolt broke out. Rome sent its legions. Inside Jerusalem, rival Jewish factions fought one another even while the city was under siege, and Josephus describes the famine inside the walls in harrowing detail. In the end the Romans broke through, and the Temple, Herod's beautiful house, burned. The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, remembers the day: the ninth of Av, the same date tradition gives for the fall of the First Temple. Then the rabbis asked the question that follows a disaster: why? Their answers look somewhere unexpected. In the Bar Kamtza story, the humiliated guest goes to the Roman authorities and stirs up suspicion against Jerusalem. And when the rabbis might have stopped the plot, one rabbi's overcareful scruples held them back; the Talmud says that rabbi's humility destroyed the house and burned the sanctuary. And in tractate Yoma, the rabbis say the Second Temple was destroyed because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred, people hating one another for nothing. Rome lit the fire. The rabbis didn't deny that. But they turned the question inward, toward how people treated each other at the table. The book of Lamentations, read on the ninth of Av, opens with the grief of an empty city: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" The ninth of Av is still kept with a fast, with mourners sitting low, and with those words read aloud.
screen: `JUDEA REVOLTS AGAINST ROME.` · `THE CITY FIGHTS ITSELF UNDER SIEGE.` · then, large: `THE TEMPLE BURNS ON THE NINTH OF AV.` · then: `THE RABBIS ASK WHY: BASELESS HATRED.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with a loss. Sit low if you can, on a cushion or the floor, the way mourners sit on the ninth of Av. Let your hands rest. Let one loss come to mind, big or small, recent or long ago: a person, a place, a version of your life that ended. Don't try to fix it or explain it. Just let it be in the room with you, and keep breathing. If a cause comes to mind, notice whether part of it was between people. If you pray, you can say the line from Lamentations: how doth the city sit solitary. The bell holds the time.
The Great Revolt. Judea rose against Rome, the city fought itself, and the Temple burned. The rabbis looked for the cause in baseless hatred. Today's word.
Your line: the second temple fell. Today, if you see someone left out or shamed, don't be the one who says nothing. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: Masada
900.hook: the last stronghold falls, and what it means is still argued
900.howItsDone: Masada is visited as a historical site in Israel; Jewish readers, teachers and historians continue to debate what its story, known from Josephus, should mean.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Great Revolt, and a Talmud story that begins the fall of Jerusalem with a guest thrown out of a feast. Your line was the second temple fell. Did you speak up for anyone? Today, the war's last chapter, on a rock in the desert. Day nine hundred.

A flat-topped mountain rises out of the desert near the Dead Sea, with cliffs on every side. Herod had built a palace fortress on top, with storerooms and cisterns cut into the rock. Jewish rebels had seized it early in the war, and after Jerusalem fell they still held it. Rome came after them, camped below, and built a great ramp up the side of the mountain so their siege engines could reach the wall. The name of the place is Masada. What happened at the top is still argued over, and the story comes to us through one writer.
screen: `A ROCK IN THE DESERT.` → `REBELS HOLD HEROD'S FORTRESS.` → `ROME BUILDS A RAMP.`

segments.voice: That writer is Josephus, in the last book of his Jewish War. He tells it this way. When the Romans breach the wall and the end is certain, the rebels' leader, Eleazar ben Yair, gathers the defenders. In two long speeches he urges them to choose death for themselves and their families rather than be enslaved. Josephus says the men killed their own families, then each other by lot, and the last man killed himself. When the Romans break in the next morning, ready for battle, they find silence. Josephus says a few women and children hid and survived, and that it was from them the story became known. Now the argument. For some readers, Masada stands for courage: people who would not be slaves. For others, the story raises hard questions. They point to the weight Jewish law gives to every life, including one's own, and ask whether this was heroism or tragedy. Historians ask a different question: how much of the story, and of those speeches, is Josephus's own telling, written in Rome after the war, about a group he describes elsewhere in harsh terms. And some point out that the Masada story isn't one the rabbis tell; it reaches us from Josephus. All of these readers are looking at the same rock. The tradition doesn't hand us one tidy meaning. What it hands us is one writer's account, and readers who still argue over it.
screen: `JOSEPHUS TELLS THE STORY.` · then, large: `THEY WOULD NOT BE SLAVES.` · `COURAGE, OR TRAGEDY?` · then: `HOW MUCH IS JOSEPHUS?`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hold one story people disagree about. Sit and let your breath steady. Choose one story from your family, your town, or your own past that different people tell differently. Hold the version you usually tell. Then set it gently to one side and hold another version, the way someone else might tell it. Don't pick a winner. Notice that both are about the same mountain. Breathe with both. If you pray, you can bring that story and the people in it to God without settling it. The bell holds the time.
Masada. Herod's desert fortress, the rebels' last stand against Rome, told by Josephus, and argued about ever since: courage, tragedy, or a story shaped by its teller. Today's word.
Your line: masada. Today, when a story comes up that people disagree about, ask one person how they tell it, and just listen. Day nine hundred.

901.title: From Temple to study
901.hook: at Yavneh, Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuilds Jewish life around study and prayer
901.howItsDone: Jewish prayer services follow a daily rhythm that the Talmud connects to the Temple offerings, and Torah study, in a synagogue, a study hall or at home, is itself treated as a form of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Masada: a fortress on a desert rock, and a story still argued over. Your line was masada. Did you hear someone tell a story their way? Today, while Jerusalem is still under siege, a teacher gets out in a coffin. Day nine hundred one.

The coffin is carried to the city gate by two students, one at the head and one at the feet. The guards inside Jerusalem want to stab it, to be sure the body is dead. The students talk them out of it. Inside the coffin is their teacher, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, very much alive. That's how the Talmud, in tractate Gittin, tells his escape from the besieged city. He has pretended to be sick, then pretended to die, because the zealots holding Jerusalem won't let anyone leave. Once outside, he walks to the Roman commander's tent with one request.
screen: `A COFFIN AT THE CITY GATE.` → `THE TEACHER INSIDE IS ALIVE.` → `HE WALKS TO THE ROMAN TENT.`

segments.voice: In the Talmud's story the Roman is Vespasian, soon to become emperor, and he tells the rabbi to ask him for something. Among his requests, Rabbi Yochanan asks, in paraphrase: give me Yavneh and its sages. Yavneh. Not Jerusalem. Not the Temple. A place to keep teaching. The Talmud doesn't pretend everyone agreed with him. It records a sharp objection: he should have asked Rome to spare Jerusalem itself. And it gives his reasoning: ask for that much, and he might not get even a little rescue. Now think about what had just been lost. Until then, Jewish worship had a center: one house, one altar, priests, offerings. With the Temple burned, what could take its place? At Yavneh, tradition says, the sages began to answer: study of Torah, and prayer. The Talmud links the daily prayers to the daily Temple offerings, so that the words a person says stand where the offering once stood. Long before, the prophet Hosea had already pointed this way: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." The same verse ends with an offering of a new kind; in the Hebrew, it is bulls of our lips. Words, in place of bulls. A sanctuary made of time and speech, which can be carried anywhere. In the rabbis' telling, that move, from Temple to study, is how a people without a Temple kept going. The house was gone. The conversation went on.
screen: `GIVE ME YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.` · `SOME SAID HE SHOULD HAVE ASKED MORE.` · then, large: `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` · then: `A SANCTUARY YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to rebuild one thing after a loss. Sit, and breathe slowly. Choose something that changed and can't go back to the way it was: a job, a home, a routine, a friendship, a way your body used to work. Then ask Rabbi Yochanan's question. Not "how do I get the whole city back?" but "what is my Yavneh?" What is one small thing I can still build, here, that carries what mattered? Let one answer come. It can be very small. If you pray, you can take with you words, as Hosea says, and return. The bell holds the time.
From Temple to study. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asks Rome for Yavneh and its sages, and Jewish life is rebuilt around Torah study and prayer. Today's word.
Your line: from temple to study. Today, after something doesn't go your way, ask what your Yavneh is, and build that one small thing. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: The table is the altar (Berakhot 55a)
902.hook: the Talmud says that now a person's table atones, through hospitality
902.howItsDone: In Jewish homes that keep the custom, the bread blessed at the start of a meal is touched to salt, a custom linked to the salted Temple offerings, and welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, is counted a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a teacher carried out of Jerusalem in a coffin, asking Rome for Yavneh and its sages. Your line was from temple to study. Did you find your Yavneh? Today, the rabbis find an altar somewhere unexpected. Day nine hundred two.

A plate of bread, a small dish of salt. At some Jewish tables, before the meal begins, someone says the blessing over the bread, breaks it, and touches each piece to the salt before passing it around. It looks like a simple kitchen habit. Tradition ties it to a memory. In the Torah, the offerings brought to the altar were salted: "with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt." The altar is gone. The salt is still on the table. And the Talmud has a line about where the altar went.
screen: `BREAD AND A DISH OF SALT.` → `THE OFFERINGS WERE SALTED.` → `WHERE DID THE ALTAR GO?`

segments.voice: It's in tractate Berakhot, page fifty-five. The passage starts with a list of things that lengthen a person's days, and one of them is lingering long at your table. Why would that be? The Talmud explains: because a poor person might come, and you'll be there to feed them. Then two teachers, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar, both say, in paraphrase: as long as the Temple stood, the altar atoned for Israel. Now that it's gone, a person's table atones for them. The rabbis anchor this in a verse from Ezekiel's vision of the future Temple. The verse begins by describing an altar of wood, and then, in the same breath, it calls the thing a table: "This is the table that is before the LORD." The rabbis noticed that it starts as an altar and ends as a table. The commentator Rashi explains how a table atones: through hospitality, by feeding guests and the hungry. So the rabbis took the altar, the center of the old worship, and set it down in the kitchen. Notice what this does with yesterday's story. At Yavneh, words stood in for offerings. Here, a meal does. The house of God is gone, so every house gets a piece of its work. And it means the measure of a table isn't the food on it. It's who has a seat. A meal shared with someone who needed one becomes, in the rabbis' language, a kind of offering. Some readers hear the salt on the bread as a small reminder of that.
screen: `LINGER AT THE TABLE: A GUEST MAY COME.` · then, large: `NOW A PERSON'S TABLE ATONES.` · `IT STARTS AS AN ALTAR, ENDS AS A TABLE.` · then: `RASHI: THROUGH HOSPITALITY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to host someone for a meal. You don't have to cook right now. Sit, breathe, and picture your own table: a dining table, a kitchen counter, a desk where you eat lunch. Who could have a seat at it this week? Someone lonely, someone new in town, a neighbor, a colleague eating alone. Let a name come. Then picture the small details: what you'd serve, where they'd sit, the bread passed hand to hand. Hold that name, and decide one step: a message, an invitation, an extra sandwich. If you pray, you can say a blessing you know before your next meal. The bell holds the time.
The table is the altar. With the Temple gone, the Talmud says a person's table atones, and Rashi explains how: by feeding guests and the hungry. Today's word.
screen: `THE TABLE IS THE ALTAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the table is the altar. Today, set one extra place, or invite one person to eat with you this week. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: Bar Kokhba (132–135 CE)
903.hook: a second revolt is crushed, and Jews are barred from Jerusalem
903.howItsDone: The fall of Betar is remembered on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, alongside the destruction of both Temples, in the fast and the readings of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salt on the bread and an altar that moved into the kitchen. Your line was the table is the altar. Did anyone get a seat at yours? Today, the week ends with a second revolt against Rome, and a hope that rose very high. Day nine hundred three.

"There shall step forth a star out of Jacob." That's a line from the book of Numbers, spoken by Balaam, a promise of a ruler rising from Israel. Years after the Temple burned, a new Jewish commander rose up against Rome. And Rabbi Akiva, a teacher honored by the sages, looked at him and reached for that verse. His name was Koziba, and Akiva read it into the verse: not a star, but Koziba, steps forth out of Jacob. When he saw the man, Akiva said: this is the king, the anointed one. The fighter became known as Bar Kokhba, son of a star.
screen: `"A STAR OUT OF JACOB."` → `AKIVA POINTS TO A COMMANDER.` → `SON OF A STAR.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Jerusalem Talmud, in tractate Taanit. Not everyone in the study hall agreed with Akiva. Another sage, Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta, answered him with a sharp, sad line, in paraphrase: Akiva, grass will grow out of your cheeks, and the son of David still won't have come. In other words: you'll be long buried before the redemption arrives, and this isn't it. The revolt was crushed. The Mishnah, in the same list of grief we met with the Temple's fall, records that on the ninth of Av the fortress of Betar was captured. Rome made Jerusalem a Roman city with a new name, Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were barred from entering it. Other rabbinic passages call the commander simply Bar Koziba, and some readers hear in it son of a lie, a bitter play on the same name. One man, two nicknames, and the gap between them is the story. The rabbis didn't hide that their honored teacher backed a hope that failed. They kept Akiva's words and Yochanan ben Torta's answer side by side, the way they kept Hillel and Shammai. The page leaves a question for whoever reads it: what do you do with a hope that failed? Akiva's words are still there, and so is the answer that told him he was wrong.
screen: `GRASS WILL GROW FROM YOUR CHEEKS.` · `BETAR FALLS ON THE NINTH OF AV.` · then, large: `SON OF A STAR, SON OF A LIE.` · then: `THE RABBIS KEEP THE MISTAKE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit honestly with a defeat. Sit still and let your breath go slow. Let one hope come back to you, one that didn't come true: a plan, a person you trusted, a cause you were sure of. Say plainly, inside: this didn't work. Don't add a reason, and don't add a lesson yet. Just let it be true for a few breaths. Then notice that you are still here, still breathing, after it. As the week closes, look back too: a wall, two schools, a fall, a fortress, a coffin, a table. If you pray, you can bring the hope that failed to God. The bell holds the time.
Bar Kokhba. Son of a star, Akiva called him; the revolt was crushed, Betar fell, and Jews were barred from Jerusalem. The rabbis kept the hope and the failure on the record. Today's word.
Your line: after the revolt. Today, name one thing that didn't work out, out loud to someone you trust, without dressing it up. Day nine hundred three.

fork.setup: you're a sage in the study hall. Rabbi Akiva, an honored teacher, says this commander is the promised king. what do you say?
options: agree, since Akiva said it.
tell him plainly that he's wrong.
stay quiet and wait.
fork.reveal: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torta tells him: grass will grow from your cheeks and the son of David still won't have come. the Talmud keeps both their words.

original.note: Hebrew: star, the word in "a star out of Jacob" that Akiva read as the commander's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rebel with a nickname.
what it means: a second revolt against Rome, backed by Rabbi Akiva, ends with Betar fallen and Jews barred from Jerusalem.
what a scholar hears: "son of a star" and "son of a lie" are plays on one name, and the Jerusalem Talmud records Akiva's hope beside the sage who told him he was wrong.
